utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please bring in the accused, Mr.. Registrar. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So the interpreters are ready? Are they, yes? Everyone is ready, all set? Everyone can hear me? General Blaskic, you can hear me? The parties, Defence, Prosecutor, assistants, fellow judges? Great. Well, let us resume our proceedings, I see that Mr.. Harmon is about ready to speak. Go right ahead, sir. I suppose it is a protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President and your Honours, good morning counsel. The next witness, Mr. President and your Honours, is a protected witness. I will explain to the court what the court can expect from the testimony of this witness. First, Mr. President, the witness, who will be identified as Witness M, is a Muslim resident of middle Ahmici. The witness will testify about the presence and pre-positioning of HVO troops in the village before the attack. The witness will describe the attack on her house and the killing of her husband, she will testify about large concentrations of HVO combat troops in her part of the village on the morning of April 16th 1993. She will testify about her observations of intentional fire setting to Muslim property by HVO troops. She will describe that she was used as a human shield. That is what the witness will be testifying about, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mark Harmon. Now I would like to insist on what the court is looking for in terms of testimony. Yesterday, we had three witnesses, and quite frankly I am happy to see you are setting off this morning, Mr. Harmon, because yesterday morning I had the feeling that we went straight to the essentials a little bit quicker than usual, because there was testimony and then there were questions that related only to points of clarification. We did not do quite as well -- I say "we" because we are all in this together -- we did not do quite as well yesterday afternoon, so let us see whether we can abide by what we have said we will do, that is to say the witness will give us her narrative and then you will put a number of questions. This is a public session, and I would like to recall what the point of the trial is, it is a matter of going to the essentials in the case against General Blaskic for crimes of humanity committed in the Lasva Valley region. So I suggest we begin. Mr. Registrar, if you would please have the blinds lowered, Witness M will be brought in and we will read out the solemn declaration while seated. That is the procedure we follow with protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will abide by the court's desires. I would, however, request the court's indulgence in being able to ask this witness a number of focus questions before she gets into her narrative in order to properly set up the narrative part of her testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Harmon. As you know, the judges, I am speaking on their behalf, never take a dogmatic stance while looking for the truth and for the essentials and the judges do not want to go into any investigations to one of the other tragic events and that would not be in the Tribunal's interest. I do not think any court could work along those lines. But the judges are not opposed to you putting questions, that is not the point, rather that you go into elements that emerge spontaneously, we keep all this in the transcript, but needless to say, you will ask the questions that you deem to be relevant, but insofar -- I would ask that you let the witness go ahead with her testimony. There is no point dwelling on points except for those which you deem to be essential to your case and I think all this is perfectly compatible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness M, can you hear me, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you on behalf of fellow judges for being here at the Prosecutor's office's request. Please read the solemn declaration that the Registrar is going to be putting before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Should I get up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain seated because you are a protected witness and read the declaration, please. WITNESS M (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness M. We are going to be referring to you as Witness M because you are, as I said, a protected witness. Now the Prosecutor is present here, the Defence is here, it is the Prosecution which has called you in its case against General Blaskic, who is present in the courtroom. It is a matter of testifying about events which you and unfortunately a large number of other people were affected by in the course of April 1993. The counsel for the Prosecution told us you had something to say about the HVO positions, what happened on 16th April; also in respect of how the soldiers set fire to your house; also the fact that you were taken hostage and used as a human shield. That is just a number of events, of course, you can touch on others as well. Now the counsel for the Prosecution is going to be putting a few questions to you and thereafter you will comment in your own words about the events I have just mentioned and thereafter at any point of time the counsel of the Prosecution will put, as and when necessary, questions to you. Now madam, Witness M, please look and read what is on that paper, without saying what your name is, just for the sake of identification. That is you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So then, Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness M, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am going to ask you a series of focused questions before we get to your narrative, so let me begin with those questions. How old are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you move to the village of Ahmici in October 1992 in order to care for the house and livestock of one of your husband's relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that residence located in the middle part of Ahmici just below the lower mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April 1993, were you married and did you have a three and a half year old child?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were you and your husband Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you just a quick series of questions about your husband. Was he a soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he fight against the Serbs at the front-lines near Turbe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In that regard, did he rotate to and from the front-lines from the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would that rotation include spending ten days at the front-lines, then ten days at the barracks and then ten days at your residence in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When he returned home from the front-lines, would he bring his rifle home or did he leave his rifle elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he would not bring it home. He would leave it to another soldier who would take over the shift from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He would leave it at the front-lines, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he participate in village guard duties in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When he participated in those guard duties, did he have a weapon with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, Mr. President, I would like Prosecutor's next exhibit, which is exhibit number 147, disseminated to your Honours, counsel and to the witness. I would ask that it not be placed on the ELMO. For the record, Mr. President, this is a detailed portion of one of the other exhibits, it has locations identified by number and it has a corresponding legend attached to it. Witness M, let me ask you, before coming in to testify today, did you point out a number of locations on what is the exhibit before you that will be relevant to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are those locations marked with numbers and arrows?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to check the legend and what is indicated on the legend to determine if it accurately represents what is depicted on the exhibit, the aerial photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the legend accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to direct your attention just briefly to the Tuesday before the attack on April 16th. Did you have a conversation with your husband about what he had seen at the Pican cafe and could you explain that briefly to the court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On Tuesday he came from Vitez and came by the cafe called Man, which was very close, kind of next door to Pican's cafe. He had a drink in this cafe, he saw Pican's cafe, a large number of soldiers wearing uniforms and carrying arms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those HVO soldiers he saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was he concerned and frightened about what he had seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was concerned how come there were so many soldiers there, there was no need for them to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn your attention to the night before the attack, the night of 15th April 1993. Did your husband participate in guard duties in the village of Ahmici on that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you explain to the judges what unusual observations he reported to you that he had seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 12.30, we entered the house and we each lit a cigarette, and a shot rang out, some kind of detonation rang out in the vicinity. They stepped out of the house to see what the sound was about. He came to the dugout which the HVO members had prepared and he noticed that there was a large number of soldiers in this dugout, which was unusual. He returned but he could not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the dugout indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 147 with a circle and the number 2 next to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he also report seeing anything unusual at the house of Ivica Kupreskic and could you explain to the court what he reported seeing there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he came back from the guard duty, he called me -- he wanted me to look through the window at the house next door, which was owned by Ivica Kupreskic. In the basement there were a lot of soldiers, they were armed and they were in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the house of Ivica Kupreskic indicated by the number 1 and is it circled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now Witness M, on 16th April, the morning of 16th April, were you at home with your husband, your small son and your husband's sister, who was aged approximately 20 or 21?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a pistol in the house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There were no other weapons, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now would you kindly tell the judges what happened to you and to members of your family on the morning of 16th April 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. We were awakened in the morning, we heard somebody running through the yard, I woke up, then we heard a shot and my husband was awakened and he said, "they are shooting, go and protect the child". We were in pyjamas, he was in pyjamas because we were asleep, and he went outside and at the moment he touched the knob, there was an explosion, it was probably an explosive device which had been put on the door, and then he was shot through the heart and it came out through his back and he was only able to say a word. As the shooting started through the door, at the same time the shooting started through the windows from the other side. They were shooting savagely. I took my son down to the floor and I awakened his sister and I told them to be quiet. I saw that it was 5.35 in the morning. I saw that he was hit in the heart area, and his arms were also bloodied. I saw the exit wound on his back, it was large. Then he started shivering. I managed to get some water to wash his face. Then the blood started coming out of his mouth. I turned him to the side, but there was nothing I could do. He died. I checked his pulse and here the pulse (indicates), and there was no sign of heart beat. We tried to stay composed. I knew that if we utter a voice or if we made any noise that they would come in and shoot us too. Then they threw a grenade into the room where my mother-in-law was asleep -- sorry, my sister-in-law. We were afraid. The glass on the windows was already shattered, there was still shooting going on and they were calling out, "come out, traitors. We fed you and you betrayed us". I apologised a little bit but they said, "fuck Alija", and they cursed our balijas mother and things like that. My sister-in-law proposed that we should come out and surrender. I was not prepared to surrender because I knew if we would surrender that we would be killed, both we and the child, and the shooting went on constantly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: house below was also empty. There was a bag in my room which I took, it was an empty bag, I put my robe in it and the pistol. I returned to my sister-in-law and I told her that we should jump out of the window. We were afraid, but we had no other way out, because the smoke was already coming into the room and also the dust from the bullet fire, and we were choking. I told her that I would go first. When I came back from that room, and while I was saying this to her, as I was closing the door, the door slammed, and after that there was a burst of fire and the glass shattered and another hand grenade was thrown into that room. It exploded and we were protected by the wall. We pulled back as far as we could, and then there was a lull. I saw that we had no way out, we could not use the door because we heard them out in the yard, we heard footsteps and we overheard their conversation, I was too frightened to listen to what the conversation was about. We both kissed my husband, we went to the room and I jumped through the window first. When I was about to jump, there was nobody around. As I was jumping, two soldiers approached.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness M, let me interrupt you in your narrative right there just to ask you a couple of questions to clarify. Witness M, how was your husband dressed when he approached the front door when he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband was wearing the pyjamas in which he was sleeping.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When he approached the front door, was he armed or unarmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was not armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Could you please continue then with your narrative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two soldiers approached me, one of them asked me whether I had weapons. I told him that I did not. The other one took the bag and took the pistol out and he said, "what is this?"; I said, "a pistol". They asked me whether I had any other weapons. I told them that I did not. "Do you have any grenades", I told them I did not, as we did not have any. Then my sister-in-law threw the child out of the window, which I took in my arms and then she jumped. They then asked me where my husband was, while she kept silent. I told him that they had killed him. I told them, "you killed him, what did he do to you?".(redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) I had no idea where to go, in which direction to go. I asked him, "can I please take my husband out?". They said, "no, you cannot". "May I take the shoes for my child?"; she was barefoot, in fact we were all barefoot, we had not put on any shoes. One of them told me that I could. I started for the entrance door to the house and then I saw there was a new house being built next door to where we lived. I saw about 15 soldiers. They had camouflage uniforms on and weapons. Their faces were painted black, and one of them shot at us. He said, "back", and he cursed our mothers. We went back and in order to get to the main road, I had to pass Meho Hrustanovic's house. Next to the house and in the garage, in the yard, there were between 20 to 30 HVO soldiers. They told us again to run, and I can quote them verbatim, "go now towards the wood, run. If your people start shooting at us, we will kill you", so we had to. As it was raining and we were barefoot and it was a macadam road, muddy, we slipped, but they hit us with rifle butts in our backs and (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: they took out the cow, another soldier opened a door, there was a staircase, that is where the hay was kept, and tossed in something and set the barn afire. Suad's wife and children also came out of the house and then they threw hand grenades into that house too and set it on fire. We passed his house, and we were looking for shelter where we would hide. We hid behind a house which had been under construction, was not completed, so the bottom part was finished and there was a concrete slab put on top, and that is where my sister-in-law and my child and Suad's family, his wife and his children and his father, mother, sister and their children and myself were all -- went. The father came back and saw that the barn was on fire. He wanted to let the livestock out so that it would not burn alive, but that is where he was killed. When I looked towards my house, I turned around and I could see it. The barn was on fire, the summer kitchen, the shed where we kept wood and the house itself. It was all on fire. I knew that my husband was burning. We spent a short while in this shelter, I did not see the soldiers any more, I was not even aware what was going on with me. We took the road leading to the forest and the village of Vrhovine. When we walked along that road, they shot at us. We fell down, we started crawling, there was a curve in the road and we crawled until we got into the shelter of the trees. There was a clearing of field, there was nothing there, that we had to pass. It took a long time to cover that space, but we could not, they shelled us from Hrazne, from their positions. We crawled to a barbed -- to some thorny bushes and somehow we passed through there and we reached the forest and started going towards Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right, Witness M, thank you. Let me ask you some questions now to clarify parts of your testimony. You testified that when you jumped out of your house you saw two soldiers. Can you describe what those soldiers were wearing, how they were dressed, how they were equipped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers wore camouflage uniforms, they had caps on their heads. Their faces were painted black with some kind of black cream. They were armed, they had guns, and I saw that on their belts they had grenades. The man who took my pistol away put it on his belt, like this (indicates). They had knives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You also testified, Witness M, that you saw two large groups, two concentrations of soldiers. One was approximately 15 and the other was a concentration of soldiers approximately 20 to 30. Those were two separate groups of soldiers you saw, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were those soldiers dressed in the same way that the two soldiers you have just described were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Referring to the exhibit that is in front of you, let me orient you through this exhibit. Number 3 represents the location of your residence in middle Ahmici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Number 4 represents the location where you saw these 15 heavily armed soldiers, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Number 5 is the area where you saw another group, a separate group of approximately 20 to 30 heavily armed soldiers dressed in camouflage uniforms, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The line that is in the pink, that represents the route that you and your sister-in-law and small child and others took to get away from what had happened in middle Ahmici, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were walking, fleeing the village, were you being followed by a group of soldiers immediately behind you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In your opinion, were you being used as a human shield when you were being followed by those soldiers and can you explain to the court why you believe you were being used as a human shield?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That part of the road, where they told us, "run, if your people start shooting we will kill you", it was a clearing, a meadow. There were not any houses there. Perhaps it was about 50 metres long, not more than that. Roughly about 50 metres. They used it to get to the upper part of the village of Ahmici, in order to take positions up there, because this is where Suad's house was, his father, and also there was shrubbery, there were bushes there. They took up positions there in order to get to the other part of the village of Ahmici, so that they could do up there what they did to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At a certain point, the soldiers let you proceed and then you said in your testimony, "they shot at us". Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The soldiers who were following us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you looked back toward your house, there were a number of other Muslim houses in and around your house. What was the condition of those other Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All of them were on fire, all of them were set on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There were also houses that belonged to Bosnian Croats. What was the condition of their houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These houses are undamaged until the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the court's permission I would request that we go into private session because I would like to show the witness a photograph and have her identify it. I have explained -- actually, Mr. President, we do not have to go into private session, I can do it without a private session, but I have explained to the witness that I will be showing her a photograph. I have told her about the court's concerns, she has informed me that she would like the court to have this photograph in evidence, and that she feels strong enough that she can identify it. After the identification of the photograph, Mr. President, then I will be requesting that we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, fine. We will proceed in that manner. I think the best thing would be to go straight into private session. No objection from the Defence? Fine. So Witness M, we are going to go into a private session. You are still under protection, of course. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (In open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There we go, we are in a public session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, we are not going to mention your husband's name, but generally speaking, what unit did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The 325th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The 325th. What battalion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there was a dugout, it has been circled as number 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me, is that a new dugout, or did it exist before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was newly made.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was it made?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From January to April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The night before the attack, you said that your husband was on guard with his partner Kermo and then that he came over for coffee to your place. Did he also watch television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was on television? Did you also watch it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object. I think that is outside the scope of the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I was not sure, I am not sure that that is outside the scope right now, so please do proceed, Mr. Nobilo, but do focus your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, exactly. In her examination-in-chief, the lady spoke of the evening before, so just a few more details. What was on television --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Broadcast from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am afraid that question is not illegitimate, Mr. Harmon, so please do proceed, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. So what was on television, once again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Studio Busovaca HTV from Busovaca was showing a telecast and as soon as it ended on Busovaca, then TV Vitez took this over.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see Dario Kordic, specifically, speaking? Did he say something about the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was on TV, could you tell us about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he was calling upon the Croatian people to defend themselves and he mentioned that they were attacked by the Muslim forces. He did not call the BH army "the army", he called them "the Muslim forces".

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was our defendant Tihomir Blaskic on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he say anything about that, do you remember something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was your husband's shift up?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did he hand the shift over to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he go to sleep that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he came back, he called me into the room and he asked me to look through the window to see Ivica Kupreskic's house because in the basement of that house he saw a lot of armed soldiers, which was unusual compared to other evenings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did he watch television again, listen to the radio, or did he normally go back to sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to bed, but he kept watching television and he also had a small transistor radio, battery operated, and he was listening to it, it was by his ear and I fell asleep and he woke me up once again, because he was listening to the news.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is your assessment? Was he disturbed, was he upset or was he simply listening to the news?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was quite upset after he had seen the soldiers at Pican's cafe and after everything he had seen over the past few days, he was very upset. He had a feeling that something would happen, and he kept saying that he would get killed, that he would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know whether he told the people who took over the guard from him what he saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was in Thursday -- on Thursday he was at home all day, so no one came to see us and he did not go anywhere. He was upset, he was quite upset. He was at home. He did not tell anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You did not understand me. That night, when he handed over the shift to someone else at 2400, did he tell anyone that he saw a concentration of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When the shooting started at dawn --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- did you phone someone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who did you phone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I called a friend, a lady from the upper part of the village, and I told her that my husband was wounded and that she should somehow try to get in touch with the UNPROFOR forces so that they would come and get him out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you call her husband Musa -- did you want to call her or Musa Berbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Anyone from that house. Musa was a good friend of my husband's, his father and his mother, so we were family friends. Whoever had answered the phone, I just thought it was absolutely necessary to try to call someone urgently from Vitez UNPROFOR to help my husband to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you call them? Why did you not make an urgent call? Why Musa Berbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I did not know the number. He was simply a good friend of my husband's.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When the soldiers came and when they asked about Sakib Ahmic's house, did they ask about something else, about trenches, positions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they asked, "are there any of your people in the forest? Where are your positions? Are there dugouts? Where are your trenches", et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now about the live shield. At the moment when the soldiers were following you, was there anyone shooting from upper Ahmici, the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So no one was shooting towards you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see anyone. No one was shooting, there was not any shooting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During the investigation, you did not talk about this live shield, you were just saying that the soldiers were following you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That meant that we were being used as such a shield. It was not that they were following us nicely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My colleague is telling me that the word in English should be "escorted", that the soldiers were escorting you, so it was not that they were behind you, that you were being used as a living shield. Did you talk about this living shield to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you tell them that they were accompanying you, coming with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not company when somebody is hitting you in the back with a rifle butt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that they were shooting at you. How do you explain the fact that you were not killed when you were close to them and when they were shooting at you while you were far away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we moved from the yard of Suad Ahmic, when we went along this line (indicates), you have it there in the diagram, and we were moving towards the forest and they were shooting at us. They did not want to kill us, they wanted to frighten us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see who was shooting and in what direction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, they were shooting in our direction, because they were down here (indicates) and they were shooting behind us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see who was shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just as you told us now, is that what you told the investigators too, before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to read a quotation to you and tell me whether this is what you told the investigators and whether it is true: "Ahmici was on the main road and that was the only Muslim village between Novi Travnik, Vitez and Busovaca."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the road?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you tell them that Pero Skopljak was director of TV Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute, Mr. President, may I consult with my colleague? (Pause). Another quotation, my colleague reminded me, these two soldiers, did they say, "do not shoot because there are women and children here"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Do not shoot, there are women and a child here".

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, we have thus concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecutor's office, any points of clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo asked you, Witness M, whether or not you were being "escorted" by these soldiers down the road that is indicated on the exhibit that is in front of you. Can you tell the judges in your own words what the soldiers were doing to you, what they were saying to you and what they did to you after they left your company, so we can describe this "escort" clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would just note, your Honour, it misstates my co-counsel's question. His question was, "did you tell the investigators when you were interviewed that you were escorted?".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I do not agree with you at all on that, Mr. Hayman. You yourself raised this point, which I do think is quite important. When it comes to the criminal legal terminology, since it is a matter of human shield, and you in your cross-examination, or Mr. Nobilo, had spelled out in particular as far as the translation into English goes, the use of the word "escort". Please let me finish. I do not think it is illegitimate for the counsel of the Prosecutor's office to make it clear exactly what it was the witness was trying to say. You do not look convinced, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I do not object to Mr. Harmon going into the area. My objection was that he stated in his question that Mr. Nobilo characterised the event as an escort. He did not. He asked the witness if she had characterised it as an escort when she was interviewed. He misstated my colleague's question and that was my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let us not get too bogged down by details. The main thing is to know how Witness M experienced that moment and that is what the judges would like to know, so I have taken note of your point, Mr. Hayman, so do not worry about that. You were clear. Counsel for the Prosecution, I take it then that what you are going to ask is exactly what it was that the witness experienced at the point in time in question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. Please proceed, Witness M.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I came to the house of Meho Hrustanovic and when they said we should run, run away, run towards the forest, "if your people start shooting at us", I mean at them, "we are going to kill you". That is what they said. We were walking slowly, we were barefoot, we did not have any shoes on our feet, we were slipping and they were forcing us to go faster, to run, and they were hitting us in the back with rifle butts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After they left you, then you were shot at, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They stayed in the yard of Suad Ahmic. Above Suad's house we came to a shelter, so they remained at the first house over here, they stayed here in the yard and then they were shooting after us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Mr. President. I would like to have the Exhibit 147, the accompanying legend and the photograph placed under seal, because it could indirectly identify the witness if it is public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objection? Fine, let me look at fellow judges. Judge Riad I am sure will have some points of clarification before we let Witness M go. Go right ahead, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, I will call you Witness M, I should not say your name. I would like to have some idea of where you exactly lived. You were in the middle of Ahmici, right, of the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Ahmici is a Muslim village, all of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority are Muslim houses, there are a few --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am sorry. Would you please repeat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The majority of the houses were Muslim, and a few houses marked here were owned by Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it surrounded by Croat villages or the other villages around are also majority Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Surrounded by Croat villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it is almost the only Muslim village in the centre, in the middle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said your husband saw, when he was coming from Pican's cafe, he saw large agglomerations of HV soldiers and he was very disturbed to see that. Was there any clear reason why these soldiers were coming to take their positions in Ahmici? Was there any fighting in this area? Were the Muslims attacking? Did you notice any attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No attacks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No attacks, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So the area was peaceful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was quite peaceful.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where were the Muslim forces? Do you have an idea where the Muslim forces were? Were they fighting on the front with the Serbs or were they fighting the Croats? What were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were on the front-line, they were fighting the Serbs. There was no resistance in Ahmici, if that is the word to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said that your house was burnt and all the Muslim houses when you looked were burnt, but not the Croat houses. Were these Muslim houses, to your knowledge, just houses of families living in it, or were they centres of resistance from where there were shots or anything? Were there just people living inside, children, women or concentration of people, Muslims fighting back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were Muslim houses where people lived with their families, their children, a normal life. There were not any centres of resistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Nobody started shooting from there and provoked the whole situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mentioned that while watching TV, you heard Kordic calling upon Croats to fight the Muslims, is that right? Could you precisely say what you heard, or you cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All day on television these Easter celebrations were telecast, and Kordic, Dario Kordic was making a speech. There were other people present there, and in that speech, among other things, because I was not following it non-stop, but I saw that part, my husband said, "come over and listen to this". He called upon the Croat people to fight against the Muslims. He mentioned that the Croats are attacked by Muslim forces, and he also mentioned that technically, they are superior and they could beat the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any attack from Ahmici? Were there any Muslim forces? I am sorry, I am repeating my question. Was what he said -- more or less, did it correspond to the situation on the ground and was there a Muslim attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have an idea where the people of Ahmici went after their houses were burnt? Did they stay or were they kicked out of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A few were taken away to a camp and from this part, my neighbours, quite a few were killed. The survivors fled with me. The family of Suad Ahmic, his father was killed, and I, we went towards Vrhovine. Vrhovine was a Muslim village which was free, although it was under grenade attacks on the outskirts, but there were not any soldiers in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So no Muslims were left in Ahmici after these events? Nobody could stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did people come back after that to Ahmici? Did Muslims come back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslim, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it is now being completely inhabited by Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the Muslim houses have been burned down, the Croat houses are undamaged. The Croats lead a normal life, there is not a single Muslim. They have nowhere to live because all their houses have been burned down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen? Thank you, Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness, you described some of the soldiers you saw as being in camouflage uniform. You had been in the area for some time. Can you help the court to identify these soldiers a little more clearly? Were they Muslim soldiers or Croat soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the soldiers I saw that morning were members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: They were all members of the HVO. Thank you. Defence counsel, Mr. Nobilo, asked you a question about TV shows which you saw on the night of 15th April, and I think he asked a question about General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Sorry. You gave a certain answer. Did you know General Blaskic before that date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How did you know him? Did you see him physically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know him personally. Physically, I had not seen him. Every time I saw him, I saw him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see him alone on television or in the company with others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of times when I saw him on television he was in the company of Dario Kordic and Ignjac Kostroman from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you have the impression that he belonged to the same group as Mr. Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see him on television during the day of 15th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not sure, because I was watching the part when Dario Kordic was speaking, I had housework to do, so I could not watch all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Shahabuddeen. We have concluded, Witness M. The Tribunal would like to thank you. It is quite an ordeal to come here several years later and tell us about these tragic events. We do hope that you will return home and that you will find, insofar as possible, more peace of mind. Now the court is going to take a break for 20 minutes and we will be resuming with the next witness. Thank you very much, Witness M. (The witness withdrew) (11.20 am) (A short break) (11.40 am)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The court is back in session. Have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Counsel for the Prosecutor's office, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, your Honours, good morning. The next witness is not a protected witness, her name is Habiba Pjanic. If I could say at the outset, Mr. President, your Honours, Ms. Pjanic is not feeling particularly well so I just bring that to your Honours' attention. She informed me this morning. However, she does want to proceed. With regard to the factual basis for Ms. Pjanic's testimony, she, along with her family, lived in the lower Ahmici area. The focus of her testimony, your Honours, will be directed towards the events of 16th April 1993, where her husband had departed earlier in the morning to go to the morning prayer at the mosque, which you will see from the map is directly up the street from her residence. Shortly thereafter, just after the commencement of the morning prayer, HVO soldiers came to her house, shot incendiary bullets through the house, came into the house, took her then oldest residing son, who was in the house, by the name of Muamer, up to the top floor, forced him to jump off the second floor balcony and then shot him in the head. After that murder, they continued with the youngest son, who also jumped off the balcony, but miraculously escaped. Their youngest daughter was likewise living at the residence, and the soldiers told her that she was going to be taken to the bungalow and raped at that location. However, because she was in the middle of her period at that time she was not raped, and after they lost attention, or did not keep their attention on the daughter, she escaped along with the mother and they then escaped up into Gornji Ahmici, as with the prior witness, went into a Muslim village that was outside of Pirici, by the name of Vrhovine. In addition, Mr. President, while she was there, she heard orders of HVO soldiers to burn everything, burn all the houses. We will likewise identify several photographs, Mr. President, your Honours, that we previously introduced into evidence. I have put those photographs next to the ELMO for their display and for the record, those are Exhibit 47/71 and 47/72. That is essentially the crux of the witness's testimony, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Registrar, perhaps you could ask the usher to show Ms. Habiba Pjanic in. How long do we expect her testimony to last, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I would say, Mr. President, approximately 45 minutes. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could ask, as with my colleague Mr. Harmon, several preliminary directed questions so we can focus the balance of our time on 16th April, I would appreciate it greatly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine. Can you hear me, madam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you tell the Tribunal your first and last names, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Habiba Pjanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the usher is going to provide you with the text of the solemn declaration. Would you please read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. MS. HABIBA PJANIC (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Please be seated. There is nothing to be afraid of, madam. You have shown a lot of courage to make it this far, you are under the Tribunal's protection. The counsel for the Prosecutor's office has asked you to come to court, you will be answering his questions, you are going to be telling us about what happened at the mosque, about your husband, your sons, what happened to your daughter, what you heard. So you will be providing your testimony. First you will be asking some -- you will be answering some preliminary questions from the Prosecutor, and then you will give us your own narrative about what you experienced and we will be putting some questions to you. So that would be it. Go right ahead, Mr. Kehoe. But first, if there is anything that is not all right, madam, do not be shy, let us know, we will interrupt and we will do what it takes to see that you feel better. Speak with your mind at rest. Please proceed, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Ms. Pjanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in 1943.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, are you a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Until 16th April 1993, did you and your family live in the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Ahmici and I lived there, except for one year and a half. I only spent a year and a half outside of Ahmici in my whole life. I lived there throughout my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You lived with your husband and your children, is that correct, Ms. Pjanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With my five children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: On 16th April, you were actually living with three of your children because two had gotten married and moved out, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Before we go into the events, your husband, how old is your husband today, or when was he born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1939, my husband was born in 1939.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Prior to the events of 16th April 1993, was your husband in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: What did he do in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say when it was formed. It was a short period of time, because he was a retiree and so they released him. He only spent a very short period of time there. During the conflict and before he was not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So at the time 16th April, your husband was already a retiree, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your two sons that were living with you on 16th April, Muamer and Mirza, when were they born?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muamer was born in 1972 and Mirza in 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they also in the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muamer yes, but Mirza was too young. He was under age at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And your daughter that lived with you at the time was Muamera, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, let me direct your attention to the events that began on 16th April 1993. Can you tell the judges what happened on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On 16th April 1993, my husband and I and my daughter Muamera got up for the Sabah. He went to the mosque, he unlocked the door and he wanted to lock behind him so that we would not have to get up. We waited that he come back from the Sabah. I heard a strong powerful explosion and that is when the mosque was hit. That is when they all were already praying to God, when the mosque was hit. Then shortly thereafter, my house was attacked. They started shooting at my house. My daughter was praying to God and I was preparing coffee, so that we could drink it, and a bullet flew past my head and hit the wall, and my daughter was still praying, and when she was done, I went to see what was going on with my son Muamer, who was in the other room, and he was putting on clothes. I told him, "Muamer, they are shooting from all sides", the glass was shattering all around. I said, "Muamer, my son, we have been attacked". I went to the other room to see where Mirza was. Mirza was also awakened by the shooting and he was putting on a track suit. Then we all went into the pantry. That is where we went when the first conflict happened. That is where we were waiting for our fate. Then I heard someone say -- they had come in front of the house and there was a barn there too, it was about 20 metres away and I heard them say, "burn here, burn everything that is here". They set the barn on fire and the livestock all burnt alive. I did not want to let them burn my cows, but they said, "come out", and I said I could not because we were locked inside the house. They said, "who is at home?" I said, "just myself and my children". Then a soldier came into the room and then through the hallway to the pantry, with the rifle pointed at us. His face was painted with something, I could not recognise him, and he had something on his head. He took my son Muamer from the pantry, and took him down the hallway, and he kept his rifle pointed at his head, and he took him to the room -- took him out to the balcony and I overheard him say, "jump". A few shots rang out and then he came for Mirza and myself. He left my daughter in the back pantry and told her not to move from there. When I came out to the balcony, Mirza jumped down. I saw him running across a field, there was an open field, and one of them said, "you will see, I can hit him". I did not know where to look first, whether at Mirza or Muamer, because Muamer was already dead, and I saw blood coming out of his head. At that moment, I felt lost, and he said, "jump", and I said, "no. If you are going to kill me downstairs, you might as well kill me here". I saw my life was over. When I looked again, my neighbours' houses were on fire all the way down. I saw that we were all finished. I think that I would not survive. Again he yelled at me "jump" and I said, "no. If you are going to kill me down there, you can kill me here". He said, "break the door open", it was a thick oak door, then he kicked it a few times, he could not open it, then he shot at it and he shot it open. Then he left me there, he said, "do not budge. If you move, I will kill you. You will see now what we will do to your daughter". At that moment I forgot about the death of my sons -- I thought that Mirza was killed too -- now I was focusing on what is going to happen to my daughter. I was worried, I was very thirsty, I had just gotten up. I started towards the old house so that I could get some water to drink. I was resigned that I would be killed, the bullets were flying around my head, but I decided to have a drink of water. When I came to the tap, I turned on the faucet and I started to drink. Something exploded, I do not know what it was. I sat back and then I came to, and I ran and hid behind the old house. Then I thought of going back to see what was happening to my daughter, even if I would be killed. Then I came and he was leading her and keeping his rifle against her head, the same way where he led me. She had a blue sweater and a scarf, she was in prayer and before that, she had a long dress, but they had torn everything off of her. Then I hid behind the house so that I would watch what they would do to my daughter. They took her under the balcony and she told me later that they said that they would take her to the bungalow, that they were kicking Muamer and they were asking her, "who is this?", and she said, "this is my brother", that is what my daughter said. They were kicking him in the head, in the face and they were laughing and, "I am sorry, buddy, but you are dead now, you are in God's garden picking tangerines". I again went to see what was going on with Muamera, and the soldier was taking her to the tap because she was also thirsty. They let her drink water, but she promised she would go with them. Apparently, she thought that I was somewhere around and she thought that I might not be found. I again hid behind the corner of the house, and she came to the same spot to drink water, and she asked them to let her go to her mum. The soldier told her, "your mum is dead, I killed her. She is definitely dead". She said, "please let me go". Then he told her something, I could not hear what he told her, and the livestock was burning alive, there were screams coming, the sheep and cows, and as he was going towards the barn, he ran over towards me. She saw me there, she took me by the hand and she said, "mum, run, run, they will kill you". We went to the weekend house of Osman Dzambeg, down a road. He started running after us, but he fell, the ground was slippery so he fell. Nobody followed us after that. So we hid there for a while, and then the refugees from Karaula saw us. They were in the weekend house of, what is his name, Ibro; "Habiba, run over here, through the bars in the basement", but there was shooting going on, there was a big fence, somehow we managed to get across and we got there. When we arrived there, there was Said from Morvac, and he was in the Chetnik camp before. He had a son Amir and a wife and there was Kazim and Kazim's wife and his two girls. I told them, "run, because they killed all of my family". Said said, "I am not going to wait for them, I have no teeth left in my mouth, they were all knocked out and they will break all my ribs", so he went in the direction of Gornji Ahmici and he fled by himself. I waited for my Muamera, she was resting a little bit. I started -- she could not follow me, she was waiting for the other girls who were there. I came up to a hill. When I saw there my house is on fire, all the houses on fire. It was misty, so we were able to get out, they could not see us. I went to my sister's in Gornji Ahmici, in upper Ahmici. As I was walking towards my sister's house, we were going through a clearing and the shooting was all around. I could not orient myself well, because I was very depressed, I thought that my husband was killed too, because when he was coming back from the mosque, he was wounded, but I did not know his whereabouts at the time. I came to my sister's, to the basement of my sister's son's house. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: through the wood and they were able to rescue themselves. So we all stayed there, somebody said it was 9.00, I know it was not 10.00 yet. They said that they saw -- a fire was built and we cooked some food for the children, for the little ones. They said, "they are 150 metres away from us, we have to leave here". This is between upper Ahmici and where we were, that is the mosque in the upper Ahmici, that is where we were, in the basement. When we came to upper Ahmici, a sniper was shooting and it was dark, so we hid again in the bushes, in the hedge and we entered Petko's house. We all started from there. They were holding Kratine and Borik and they went to see whether they cut it off so we could go out to Vrhovine. They came back and said that we could pass through and we did. We started, there were also elderly people whom I held, there were very small children. We arrived at Vrhovine around 12.45. That is where we spent the night, some people in the garage, some in the mosque, some wherever they could find a place. So how ever each person could find best where to spend the night, that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Pjanic. I would like to ask you a couple of questions now about the testimony that you just gave to the judges. Mr. President, your Honours, if I could first then direct the court and the witness to Exhibit 149, if we could place that on the ELMO, it is again a map of lower Ahmici with only one location designated. I do not think you have it yet, Mr. President, your Honours. Mr. Usher, if we could place that on the ELMO, please? Ms. Pjanic, you see on that map the house that is circled with the number 1 next to it. Is that the house that you lived in with your husband and three children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is. It is small. I think this is my house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, is your house relatively close to the building that you talked about before, the bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I tell about my house or any building?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Tell us about the bungalow, Ms. Pjanic. Do you know where the bungalow is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The bungalow is before my house on the main road to Travnik. That is where it is, the bungalow is, about 1,500 metres before my house, but I do not know exactly, so it is before my house. I was on an elevated ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, before the fighting, the events of 16th April 1993, did soldiers come to the bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whoever survived this incident after October, we were mistreated. We were leaving our houses, we felt unsafe. I would go to my sister's or I would go to my neighbour's or Osman Dzambeg's weekend house. We were leaving our houses because we did not feel safe. They were throwing grenades or shooting from cars at night, they were verbally abusing us. They put explosive to the house of Salkic from Nadioci and his wife and children were there and they jumped out of the windows. They destroyed him and the house with that explosive. They brought him to the mosque the next day so that we would give him a proper funeral and I saw that the son was brought a piece of his head, they said, "it was all destroyed", see they come always from the bungalow and they killed Eso. I do not know, and in front of the bungalow, they would come at night, they would bring the explosives. Ahmic Smail also left his house because soldiers came from the bungalow. They did nothing to my daughters, but they kept provoking them, they kept -- then they demolished another house and Muhamed Pezer's house, which was also there, and my sons went to help him put out the fire because he was our neighbour. The older one did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, let me stop you there and ask you a question. Did your sons go over to the bungalow and did your sons, when they went to the bungalow before the events of 16th April, recognise soldiers from the bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They never went to the bungalow, our own boys, because that is where they were going, not our own people. It was only they who were there, the Croats, and those who were passing through, the travellers, that is where they would stop off, but our own, no, they barely ever went to the bungalow. I do not know of anybody who did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did your sons tell you that they recognised some of the soldiers that were in the bungalow and that those soldiers from, not from Herzegovina but from Nadioci, Santici and Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they set Muhamed Pezer's house on fire, then the next one there was a group of refugees, this was Enver from Zenica. I do not know who it was, because the municipal government gave us the keys. They drove those people out, they threw in hand grenades, they went to Kazim Pezer's whole family, father, mother, sons, daughter-in-law, grandchildren, then they came to take this wood --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, did your sons go to talk to the soldiers about the wood and did they recognise those soldiers from the bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, only the older one, not the younger one and he talked to them and he said, "you should be ashamed, these people have been driven out of their houses, they got this wood for themselves. Why are you taking what is theirs?". That is what my older son told me he told them. He recognised them because some of them went to school with him, I do not know who it was, but he said that they were his school friends, that they were from Nadioci, from Santici, from Vitez, they were not just the outsiders, that is what my son was telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, do you know a man by the name of Dragan Papic? He used to go to the bungalow as well, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would meet him when I went to Dzemila Ahmic, because my field is right next to the main road. He was often passing there to go towards the bungalow. Earlier we used to visit each other, before the war. He did not even say, "hello", he would pass by me in a black uniform, I saw him personally. Not once, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, I am going to ask you several questions about the events of 16th April that you discussed previously. When you went outside, did you see HVO soldiers in front of your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all under the balcony. I do not know, I think that our own were being part of the Defence, I was not aware of what was going on, I do not know what was going on. I know that there was shooting all around, I could only leave by one -- from one side of the house and I saw Zahir's house, somebody was walking around there, but that was too far. He was my first neighbour, but at that point that seemed very far, because I was almost beside myself at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, let me ask you a question. How many soldiers were in front of your house, how many soldiers did you see from the balcony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When he took me out, there were maybe, five, six, maybe up to seven, I cannot say exactly, but they were around my Muamer where he was lying. I know that one of them laughed and said, "jump, the balija woman", and I saw that he had -- I did not see, he had something on his shoulder. When I saw my Muamer, I could not focus on -- I thought that they would kill me too and I lost interest in everything, I did not think that I would survive that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, did you see how these soldiers were dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, perhaps I could have told you then, it has been almost five years, I was very depressed. I do not know, I cannot. They were walking around in black uniforms most of the time. I would go to Vitez and before the conflict, I saw two trucks full of them, they were all in black, they wore something on their heads also, they were shooting. We did not have any buses, I had to go on foot, I had to go to see the doctor. They were shooting and when they came up to me, they said, "listen, you balija woman, you will not be going around here in Muslim clothes any more", but they were wearing black most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, when the soldiers took your daughter, you said that they were going to take your daughter to the bungalow, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She told me, I could not talk about it very much, because I had had enough of everything, I talked to her about it very little. She just told me that they told her that they would take her to the bungalow and she only stopped to have a drink of water. She thought she could escape that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did she tell you that the soldiers told her they were going to take her to the bungalow to rape her?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what she said. I did not talk to her about it. It was not easy for me, but that is what she was saying, that that is what was supposed to happen. Something happened to her, something bad, well, that is what it was. They could not do something. Because they tore her sweater and they took away her jewellery and they took away her headscarf and they were slapping her and they called her names.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, did your daughter tell you that the reason they did not take her to the bungalow to rape her was because she was having her period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, let me move ahead to you hiding in your sister's basement in Gornji Ahmici. You said that there were wounded people in the basement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were these wounded people civilians, women, children?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was all civilians. Not a single soldier suffered that morning. It was only civilians who were hurt or killed, our civilians, only civilians. I did not see anybody else. Munir Ahmic was killed in his pyjamas, I think. He was hit in his pyjamas, and he was killed just like my Muamer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, when you were up in Gornji Ahmici, you said that you and the other civilians were being shot at. Were you being shot at from the direction of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were shooting from the Mejtef.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Were they also shooting from the houses of Vlatko Kupreskic and Zoran Kupreskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what others said. I was not close to their house. The shooting was coming from that direction, where my sister's basement was, but where my house was, no, there was not any shooting from the Kupreskics, and I was in a corner towards the forest, but others were saying -- because we were in the basement, you know, so we could not orient ourselves where it was coming from, but people were saying it was coming from their house, people who were there, people who went out. They tried to protect us with furniture, you know, so that the grenades would not tear the walls down, but grenades were coming from all directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ms. Pjanic, if I could turn your attention to two photographs that we have discussed previously and with the assistance of the usher if I could place 47/71 on the ELMO first?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my house, this is where the soldier saw me and he said, "if you move, I will kill you" and he went back to get my daughter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The soldier put you right in front of the door, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On those steps when you get out of the house, the first landing, I went down the steps and he was pointing a gun at my head and he told me not to move, that he would go and get my daughter. He said, "you are going to see what we are going to do to your daughter".

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The next photograph, if we could, Mr. Usher, which is, for the record, 47/72. That is also a photograph of your house, is it not, Ms. Pjanic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but house -- I mean, was not photographed from the side where it was hit, only from this other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The place where your house was hit and where the balcony is, is on the other side of the house, is that right, the part that is not depicted in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the other side, I mean I went by there a few days ago, this other side looks just like the roof over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It was on this other side of the house where your son Muamer was forced to jump off and was murdered, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the side down there, I had two balconies, two fences, and it was the second floor balcony that he had to jump down from. A group of soldiers was waiting for him down there and they shot him. When I got down, he had already fallen on his face, and I saw blood coming from his head. He was cutting firewood the previous day and he fell on the wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the next exhibit is Exhibit 150 which is an exhibit which, among other people, depicts her deceased son Muamer. If I could hand that out to the court and the Defence. I have consulted with the witness on this and she has asked if I would identify her son in this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, the photograph is a photograph of her son Senus's wedding, who is in the middle of the photograph, and the son that was murdered on the morning of 16th April 1993, Muamer, is on the top row, left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is my son Muamer and this is my son Senus.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this time, Mr. President, the Office of the Prosecutor would like to offer into evidence Exhibit 149, which is the map, and the photograph Exhibit 150. At this point we have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine, thank you, counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Nobilo -- madam, the Defence counsel, one of the attorneys of General Blaskic will be putting some additional questions to you. If you need anything, we are here at your disposal and we will do whatever is necessary. Are you okay, do you feel all right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Ms. Pjanic, good day. I am Anto Nobilo, and my colleague Russell Hayman and I are defending General Blaskic. In order to clarify this situation, I would like to put a few questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Your husband, when was he mobilised? When did he join the Territorial Defence before this conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
